title: Infrastructure Configuration Validation
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of infrastructure configuration validation.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to infrastructure configuration validation.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Infrastructure Configuration Validation. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Docker Compose describes a multi-service application declaratively. It can define images/builds, networks, volumes, environment, health checks, and dependencies; startup order alone does not guarantee that a dependency is ready to accept requests. Learning infrastructure configuration validation helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Docker Compose describes a multi-service application declaratively. It can define images/builds, networks, volumes, environment, health checks, and dependencies; startup order alone does not guarantee that a dependency is ready to accept requests.

items.title: Compose-file validation
items.text: Compose declares services and shared resources together. Use `docker compose config` to inspect the resolved model before starting or deploying it.

items.title: Configuration checks
items.text: For configuration checks, name the relevant Docker object, setting, or operational step; predict its effect; and capture evidence from a controlled test or inspection command. Relate the result back to infrastructure configuration validation rather than assuming that a successful command proves the wider system is correct.

items.title: Environment-specific configuration tests
items.text: For environment-specific configuration tests, name the relevant Docker object, setting, or operational step; predict its effect; and capture evidence from a controlled test or inspection command. Relate the result back to infrastructure configuration validation rather than assuming that a successful command proves the wider system is correct.

items.title: Catching invalid mounts and ports
items.text: A container port and a published host port are different values. Bind publishing deliberately, especially when a service should be reachable only from the local machine.

items.title: Preventing configuration regressions
items.text: Operational signals should help answer what failed, when it failed, and what changed. Establish a baseline and record the checks used to decide that the service recovered.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
